title: Year 8 Maths summary and memory tips

scenes.heading: Year 8 Maths summary and memory tips
scenes.sub: A whole year of maths in two minutes
scenes.say: A whole year of maths in two minutes? Let's go. Here are the big rules from Year 8, and the memory tricks that make them stick.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Packing a school bag: only what you need for tomorrow
scenes.science: Revising: the key rules and tricks, not every page
scenes.breaks: A bag can leave things at home. A test might need any rule, so revisit any chapter that feels shaky.
scenes.say: Think of revision like packing your school bag the night before. You don't take every book, just what you need. This summary packs the key rules and the best memory tricks. If a chapter feels shaky, go back to its lessons.

scenes.heading: Number
scenes.say: Number first. When you multiply negatives, count them: an even number gives a positive answer, an odd number a negative. Brackets matter: negative three, all squared, is nine. For percentages, use multipliers: fifteen percent up is times one point one five. And for ratios, always find one part first.
scenes.caption: Number first. Multiplying negatives? Count them: even gives +, odd gives −. Brackets matter: (−3)² = 9. For percentages, use multipliers: 15% up is × 1.15. For ratios, always find one part first.

scenes.heading: F, Z and C on parallel lines
scenes.say: Here are two parallel lines and a transversal. First the seventy degree angle at the top. Angle a sits in the same position lower down, so it's corresponding: seventy degrees. Angle b is vertically opposite the seventy: also seventy. Remember F and Z angles are equal, and C angles add to one hundred and eighty.
scenes.caption: Two parallel lines and a transversal. Angle a is in the same position as 70°, so it's corresponding: 70°. Angle b is vertically opposite the 70°: also 70°. F and Z angles are equal; C angles add to 180°.

scenes.heading: Pythagoras: longest? Add. Shorter? Subtract.
notes: c is opposite the right angle
scenes.say: Now a right-angled triangle with sides six and eight centimetres. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. Square and add: thirty-six plus sixty-four is one hundred. The square root of one hundred is ten, so the hypotenuse is ten centimetres.
scenes.caption: A right-angled triangle with sides 6 cm and 8 cm. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. Square and add: 36 + 64 = 100. √100 = 10, so the hypotenuse is 10 cm.

scenes.heading: Straight-line graphs
scenes.say: Straight-line graphs: y equals m x plus c. m is the gradient, rise over run, and c is where the line crosses the y-axis. So y equals three x plus one is steep, with gradient three, and crosses the y-axis at one.
scenes.caption: Straight-line graphs: y = mx + c. m is the gradient, rise ÷ run, and c is where the line crosses the y-axis. So y = 3x + 1 has gradient 3 and crosses the y-axis at 1.

scenes.heading: Two rules people forget
scenes.say: Two rules people forget. Index laws: when you multiply, add the indices; divide, subtract; a bracket, multiply. And anything to the power zero is one. For inequalities, solve like an equation, but if you multiply or divide by a negative, flip the sign.
scenes.caption: Index laws: multiply → add the indices; divide → subtract; bracket → multiply. Anything to the power 0 is 1. Inequalities: solve like an equation, but × or ÷ by a negative flips the sign.

points: F and Z equal, C adds to 180°
y = mx + c: m steepness, c crossing
scenes.say: Quick recap. Count the negatives for the sign. On parallel lines, F and Z angles are equal and C angles add to one eighty. Use multipliers for percentages. For Pythagoras: longest side, add; shorter side, subtract. And in y equals m x plus c, m is the steepness and c is the crossing. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: Quick recap. Count the negatives for the sign. F and Z angles are equal; C angles add to 180°. Use multipliers for percentages. Pythagoras: longest side, add; shorter side, subtract. In y = mx + c, m is steepness and c is the crossing. Now try the practice questions!
